name: Verificationism
statement: A statement is meaningful only if it can be verified by experience, or is true by definition.
statementAccent: only if it can be verified by experience
meaning: Verificationism, or the verifiability theory of meaning, is the doctrine, central to logical positivism and the Vienna Circle, that a statement is cognitively or factually meaningful only if it is either analytic, true or false by virtue of the meanings of its words, as in logic and mathematics, or empirically verifiable, capable in principle of being verified or confirmed by sense experience. Statements that are neither analytic nor empirically verifiable are declared cognitively meaningless, not false but lacking factual sense. A common slogan is that the meaning of a statement is its method of verification. The Vienna Circle, a group of philosophers and scientists in Vienna in the 1920s and 1930s, including Moritz Schlick, Rudolf Carnap, and Otto Neurath, and influenced by Wittgenstein's Tractatus, by Russell, Mach, and Hume, set out this program, expressed in their 1929 manifesto The Scientific Conception of the World, and A. J. Ayer popularized it in the English-speaking world in his 1936 book Language, Truth, and Logic. Verificationism was above all an anti-metaphysical weapon: statements of traditional metaphysics, theology, and, on the emotivist view, ethics, being neither analytic nor verifiable, were dismissed as cognitively meaningless pseudo-statements. The criterion proved extremely hard to formulate correctly and faced a famous self-refutation objection, and it declined by the mid twentieth century.
mechanism: Verificationism ties meaning to the conditions under which a statement could be confirmed by experience. On the positivist picture, meaningful statements come in just two kinds. Analytic statements, including the truths of logic and mathematics, are true or false solely by virtue of the meanings of their terms and carry no factual content, being in effect tautologies. Synthetic statements, which purport to describe the world, are meaningful only if they are empirically verifiable, that is, only if some possible sense experience could count for or against them; where no observation could bear on a statement, it says nothing about the world and is cognitively meaningless. The meaning of such a statement was even identified with its method of verification. Applied as a criterion of demarcation between sense and nonsense, this dissolves large tracts of traditional philosophy: assertions about God, the Absolute, or a supersensible reality, being unverifiable, come out not as false but as meaningless, and ethical utterances were reinterpreted, by emotivism, as expressions of attitude rather than fact-stating claims. The great difficulty was to state the criterion precisely. Strong verifiability, requiring conclusive verification, proved too restrictive, since universal scientific laws, such as all copper conducts electricity, cannot be conclusively verified by any finite set of observations, and statements about the remote past or distant regions are also caught. Weak verifiability, requiring only that a statement be confirmable to some degree, as in Ayer's formulations of 1936 and 1946, proved too permissive, letting metaphysical statements back in, and Carl Hempel, in his 1950 survey, showed that successive versions either excluded good science or admitted nonsense.

examples.text: Only analytic statements, true by definition, and empirically verifiable statements count as cognitively meaningful.
Claims about God or the Absolute, being unverifiable, are dismissed not as false but as cognitively meaningless.
The verification principle is itself neither analytic nor empirically verifiable, so by its own standard it is meaningless.

variants.name: Strong versus weak verifiability
variants.text: Requiring conclusive verification, which is too restrictive, versus mere confirmability, which is too permissive.

variants.name: Emotivism about ethics
variants.text: The positivist recasting of ethical statements as expressions of attitude rather than cognitively meaningful claims.

whyItMatters: Verificationism was the beating heart of logical positivism, one of the most important philosophical movements of the twentieth century, and its criterion of meaning shaped debates about science, language, and metaphysics for decades. By proposing that only the analytic and the empirically verifiable count as cognitively meaningful, the Vienna Circle sought to put philosophy on a rigorous, scientific footing and to sweep away what it regarded as the empty pseudo-problems of traditional metaphysics, theology, and speculative ethics. The program powerfully expressed the empiricist demand that meaningful claims answer to experience, and it deeply influenced the philosophy of science, the theory of meaning, and the analytic tradition, even as its own central principle ran into trouble. The story of its decline is itself instructive: the repeated failure to formulate the criterion so as to admit good science while excluding metaphysics, the devastating self-refutation objection that the principle is meaningless by its own lights, Quine's attack on the analytic-synthetic distinction it relied on, and Popper's preference for falsifiability as a criterion of science rather than meaning, together brought verificationism down. As the doctrine that meaning is tied to verification, it is a pivotal episode in modern philosophy, important both for its ambitions and for the lessons of its collapse.

working.text: ask whether it is analytic, true by definition, or a synthetic claim about the world.
for a synthetic claim, require that some possible experience could confirm or disconfirm it, else count it meaningless.
dismiss unverifiable non-analytic statements, such as those of speculative metaphysics, as cognitively meaningless.

limits: Verificationism collapsed under a set of powerful objections that its proponents could not overcome. The formulation problem proved intractable: strong, conclusive verifiability excluded universal scientific laws and statements about the past, the very science positivism meant to vindicate, while weak, confirmability-based versions, including Ayer's, were shown to let virtually any statement, including metaphysical ones, count as meaningful, and Carl Hempel's 1950 review documented the repeated failures. The most damaging objection is self-refutation: the verification principle itself is neither analytic nor empirically verifiable, so by its own criterion it is cognitively meaningless, and attempts to save it, for instance by treating it as a proposal or convention rather than a substantive claim, weakened its force. W. V. O. Quine's attack on the analytic-synthetic distinction undercut one of the two categories the criterion relied on, and Karl Popper argued that falsifiability, not verifiability, marks off science, and, crucially, that unfalsifiable statements are not thereby meaningless, separating the demarcation of science from a theory of meaning. Some datings and details reward care, such as the 1929 manifesto, Ayer's 1936 and 1946 editions, and Carnap's critiques of metaphysics. So verificationism robustly tied meaning to verification, understood as an influential doctrine undone by the formulation problem, the self-refutation objection, and Quine's and Popper's criticisms.
misreadings: Verificationism does not say that unverifiable statements are false; it says they are cognitively meaningless, lacking factual sense altogether. It is not the same as Popper's falsifiability, which Popper offered as a criterion of scientific demarcation, not of meaning, and which does not brand unfalsifiable claims meaningless. And the criterion was never successfully formulated, so it is not a settled result, so treating verificationism as calling metaphysics false, as identical to falsificationism, or as a secure principle, misreads the doctrine.
origin: The logical positivist doctrine, central to the Vienna Circle and popularized by A. J. Ayer's Language, Truth, and Logic (1936), that a statement is cognitively meaningful only if analytic or empirically verifiable, used to reject metaphysics and later abandoned.

sources.text: Vienna Circle, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the Vienna Circle and logical positivism, the verifiability criterion that synthetic statements are cognitively meaningful only if empirically testable, the anti-metaphysical program, the 1929 manifesto, and the influence of Wittgenstein and Ayer.
